result: The study identified J8 and J9 as clonally related broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) that potently neutralize DENV1-4 in the low picomolar range, with major recognition determinants in E protein domain I (DI), distinct from previously characterized bNAbs. B cell repertoire analysis revealed divergent evolution of J8 and J9, suggesting multiple evolutionary pathways to generate bNAbs within this lineage.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 describe the main findings of the study. The characterization of 28 antibodies (C51), identification of J8/J9 as potent bNAbs (C52), mapping of epitopes to DI (C53), divergent evolution analysis (C54), and identification of viral/host determinants (C55) are all supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including neutralization assays, epitope mapping, and repertoire sequencing.

result: Two patients were characterized: patient 013 (31-year-old female, secondary DENV4 infection, developed severe dengue) and patient 020 (24-year-old female, primary DENV1 infection). From these patients, 15 clonal families comprising 38 unique paired VH/VL IgG1 plasmablast sequences were identified, with varying degrees of somatic hypermutation. One clonal family included members from both patients, suggesting convergent evolution.
evaluation: Claims C56-C76 describe patient characteristics and initial antibody identification. These are well-documented in Table 1 and the text, with clear clinical data, infection status, and sequencing results. The convergent evolution observation (C60) is supported by data and appropriate citations to similar phenomena in other viral infections.

result: Of 36 paired VH/VL sequences cloned into expression vectors, 28 produced detectable secreted IgG. Functional screening showed 17 antibodies bound DENV2 E protein and/or virus particles, none neutralized ZIKV, all 28 neutralized at least one DENV serotype, 21 neutralized two or more DENV serotypes, and one neutralized WNV. Six antibodies were selected for detailed characterization based on neutralization breadth.
evaluation: Claims C62-C68, C77 describe the initial functional screening results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The data clearly support these quantitative findings about antibody expression, binding, and neutralization profiles. The selection criteria for further characterization are explicitly stated and justified.

result: Binding characterization revealed that L8, M1, B10, and I7 bound both DENV2 soluble E and virus particles, while J9 and C4 bound only virus particles, suggesting these target epitopes preferentially displayed on intact virions. Incubation at 37°C modestly increased binding for most antibodies. J9 and C4 showed relatively high EC50 values (200 and 1200 ng/ml respectively), suggesting limited affinity maturation.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80, C83 describe binding assay results shown in Figure 1. The data clearly demonstrate differential binding patterns between antibodies and between soluble E versus virus particles. The inference about epitope location (C79) is reasonable based on the binding data, though structural confirmation would strengthen this conclusion. The EC50 values and interpretation about affinity maturation are directly supported by Figure 1D.

result: Neutralization assays revealed varying potencies: M1, B10, and L8 showed modest, incomplete neutralization (IC50 721-1670 ng/ml) with 10-50% residual infectivity at 10 μg/ml. I7 displayed unusual serotype specificity. C4 completely neutralized DENV1-4 but with modest potency (IC50 >1000 ng/ml for DENV4). J9 was the most potent, completely neutralizing DENV1-4 with IC50 values of 6-39 ng/ml, showing up to 60-fold greater potency than EDE1 C10 against some serotypes and up to 14-fold higher potency than EDE2 B7.
evaluation: Claims C84-C92 describe neutralization data shown in Figure 2. The IC50 values, completeness of neutralization, and comparative potencies are all directly supported by the dose-response curves and quantitative data. The interpretation of incomplete neutralization for fusion loop antibodies (C86) is supported by appropriate citations. All quantitative comparisons are backed by experimental data.

result: J9 and J8 retained potent neutralizing activity as Fab fragments, unlike C4 and EDE1 C10 which failed to achieve 50% neutralization. J9 and J8 neutralized recently isolated DENV1-4 strains (2004-2007) with IC50 <50 ng/ml and neutralized DENV regardless of virion maturation state. J9, J8, and EDE1 C10 potently inhibited DENV2 infection both pre- and post-virus attachment, while C4 failed to inhibit 40-50% of infection post-attachment even at 300 μg/ml.
evaluation: Claims C94-C99 describe additional neutralization characteristics shown in Figure 2 supplements. The Fab neutralization data (C94-C95) demonstrate epitope accessibility differences. Testing against recent isolates (C96) and different maturation states (C97) addresses important questions about antibody breadth. The pre/post-attachment data (C98-C99) provide mechanistic insights. All claims are directly supported by experimental data in the supplementary figures.

result: ADE assays in K562 cells showed all DENV-specific antibodies caused dose-dependent enhancement. J9 and J8 had the lowest peak enhancement titers for DENV2 (3 ng/ml), approximately 27-fold and 480-fold lower than EDE1 C10 (80 ng/ml) and C4 (1467 ng/ml), respectively. For J9 and J8, neutralization occurred beyond peak enhancement with no infectivity at high concentrations, while C4 and L8 showed persistent ADE at 10 μg/ml. J9 and J8 did not enhance ZIKV or WNV infection, while EDE bNAbs enhanced ZIKV and L8 enhanced both ZIKV and WNV.
evaluation: Claims C100-C108 describe ADE potential shown in Figure 3. The peak enhancement titers and fold-differences are quantitatively supported by the data. The observation that J9/J8 neutralization occurs beyond peak enhancement (C103) is important for vaccine design and is clearly demonstrated. The specificity differences for ZIKV/WNV enhancement (C105-C107) are well-documented. The conclusion about J9/J8 being desirable antibodies (C108) is a reasonable inference from the narrow ADE window.

result: Shotgun mutagenesis epitope mapping revealed that M1 and L8 lost binding to W101A and F108A mutations in the DII fusion loop, with M1 also depending on G106 and residue 75 on the bc loop. I7 epitope involved DII residues Q256 and G266, which are conserved among flaviviruses and important for recognition by antibody d448. Fusion loop specificity likely contributes to incomplete neutralization by M1 and L8.
evaluation: Claims C109-C113 describe epitope mapping results shown in Figure 4A-B. The mutagenesis data clearly identify critical residues for M1, L8, and I7 binding. The conservation of Q256/G266 (C113) is supported by sequence alignment data and citation. The inference about incomplete neutralization (C111) is reasonable and supported by citations to similar observations with other fusion loop antibodies.

result: For J9, most E protein mutations reducing binding >80% were in DI (R2, I4, K47, S145, H149, N153, T155), with additional contributions from DII G102, N242, and DIII N366. These mutations minimally affected EDE1 C10 binding. Neutralization studies confirmed N153 or T155 mutations abrogated J9 neutralization, N242 reduced potency 5-fold, and K47T+V151T reduced potency ~100-fold. Similar mutations affected J8 and C4. V151T mutations increased EDE1 C10 potency 25-fold but had minimal effects on EDE2 B7 or patient sera, suggesting no global antigenicity changes. These results indicate J9, J8, and C4 recognition determinants are distinct from EDE-specific bNAbs.
evaluation: Claims C114-C125 describe comprehensive epitope mapping shown in Figures 4-5. The binding screen data (C114) identify critical residues, and neutralization assays with mutant viruses (C116-C121) confirm their functional importance. The differential effects on EDE antibodies (C122-C124) demonstrate epitope distinctness. The lack of effect on polyclonal sera (C123) is an important control showing mutations don't globally disrupt structure. The conclusion about distinct recognition determinants (C125) is well-supported by the totality of mutagenesis data and appropriate citations.

result: B cell repertoire analysis of patient 013 PBMCs showed 8-fold more unique VH sequences from stimulated versus unstimulated cells, with greater IgG representation. VH1-69, VH3-30, VH3-30-3, VH4-34, VH4-39, and VH4-59 were dominant families. The J9/J8 lineage (579 and 43,179 VH sequences in unstimulated and stimulated PBMCs, respectively) derived from IGHV1-69+IGHD2-2+IGHJ5 recombination with no CDRH3 insertions/deletions. The lineage was predominantly IgG1 with no IgM >2 UMI counts. Clones 100% identical to J9 and J8 were found in stimulated repertoire. The rapid expansion of class-switched, hypermutated IgG strongly suggests J8 and J9 derived from memory B cells from prior infection. Divergent evolution of J9 and J8 suggests multiple somatic hypermutation pathways leading to bNAbs.
evaluation: Claims C126-C135 describe repertoire analysis shown in Tables 2-3 and Figure 6. The quantitative differences between stimulated/unstimulated PBMCs (C126-C127) are clearly documented. The lineage characteristics (C129-C132) are directly supported by sequencing data. The inference about memory B cell origin (C133) is reasonable given the high mutation levels and class switching, and is supported by appropriate citations. The observation of divergent evolution (C135) is evident from the phylogenetic tree and represents an important finding about multiple pathways to bNAbs.

result: J8 and J9 VH derived from IGHV1-69+IGHD2-2+IGHJ5 recombination, and both used IGKV3-11+IGKJ2 light chains with identical CDR lengths and no convergent germline mutations. Germline-reverted J8/J9 IgGs had no neutralizing activity, and pairing germline VH with mature VL (or vice versa) also failed to neutralize, indicating both chains require somatic hypermutation. Five CDR-H2/H3 mutations (I53F, T99P, D100cH, Q61D, K62N) were sufficient for J8 to neutralize all DENV1-4 and for J9 to neutralize DENV1-2. Additional J9 VH and VL mutations were required for DENV3-4 neutralization. The FR2 glycine insertion in J9 VH was not necessary for neutralizing activity.
evaluation: Claims C136-C143 describe germline reversion experiments shown in Figure 7. The gene usage data (C136-C137) are directly from sequencing. The germline reversion experiments (C138-C139) clearly demonstrate the requirement for somatic hypermutation in both chains. The identification of five key mutations (C140) and their differential effects on J8 versus J9 (C141) provide important insights into maturation pathways. The chimeric antibody experiments (C142) further dissect VH versus VL contributions. All conclusions are directly supported by neutralization data with the various antibody variants.

result: The study defines a new vulnerable site on the DENV E protein in domain I that can be exploited for immunogen design to elicit bNAbs.
evaluation: Claim C148 is a summary conclusion supported by the epitope mapping data (C114-C125) showing J9/J8 target DI residues distinct from previously characterized bNAbs. The potent neutralization (C89-C92), low ADE potential (C101-C103), and activity against diverse strains (C96) support this as a promising vaccine target. However, this remains a proposal for future work rather than demonstrated vaccine efficacy.

result: All human bNAbs against flaviviruses identified from natural infection were isolated from individuals with sequential exposure to ≥2 DENV serotypes. Sequential infection has been shown to broaden neutralizing responses. The high somatic hypermutation in J9/J8 at day 4 post-fever suggests recall response, though earlier timepoint analysis would be needed to confirm further maturation during secondary infection. Despite presence of bNAbs like J9/J8, donors developed severe dengue, likely because antibodies appeared too late (day 4 post-fever, 1 day before severe disease). J9/J8-like bNAbs appear to be a minor component of the polyclonal response and the J9/J8 clonal family was not the largest in patient 013's acute-phase repertoire.
evaluation: Claims C150-C158 discuss the context and implications of bNAb development. The observation about sequential infection (C150-C152) is supported by appropriate citations. The inference about recall response (C153) is reasonable but explicitly notes the limitation of single timepoint analysis. The observation about severe disease despite bNAbs (C154-C155) is important and well-documented. The minor contribution to polyclonal response (C157-C158) is supported by data in Figure 5 supplement 4 and Table 3. These claims appropriately distinguish between what is demonstrated versus inferred.

result: The introduction and discussion provide extensive background on DENV biology, disease epidemiology, vaccine challenges, antibody responses including ADE, flavivirus structure, and prior work on bNAbs. This includes established knowledge about DENV classification, transmission, disease progression, the role of pre-existing antibodies in severe disease, E protein structure and function, and limitations of current vaccine approaches. The discussion contextualizes findings within the field and proposes implications for vaccine design.
evaluation: Claims C1-C50, C144-C147, C149, C159 provide background context and are appropriately supported by citations to published literature or represent established scientific knowledge. These claims set up the rationale for the study and interpret findings in context. While not representing new experimental results from this study, they are accurately stated and properly referenced. Claim C159 about masking immunodominant epitopes is speculative but appropriately qualified and cited.
